problem_in_depth:
Start with the one fact that governs everything in this chapter: a modern chip can do arithmetic almost unimaginably fast, but it spends most of its life waiting for numbers to arrive. Adding two numbers together takes a chip a fraction of a billionth of a second. Fetching those two numbers from the chip's main memory, a few centimeters away on the board, can take a hundred times longer. Fetching them from a disk, or from another computer across the room, takes millions of times longer. So the real cost of computing is almost never the thinking. It is the fetching, the shipping, the copying, and the waiting. If you remember only one idea from this whole book, remember this: computers are limited by moving data around, not by doing the math.

Every other chapter in this book attacks that problem head-on, by building a specialized chip that keeps the data close to where the math happens. This chapter is about everything else. It is the collection of quieter, less glamorous problems that surround the fast chip and decide whether all that speed actually turns into useful work. Think of a Formula 1 car. The engine gets the headlines, but the race is won or lost on the pit crew, the fuel strategy, the tires, and whether the timekeeper is even measuring lap times correctly. This chapter is the pit crew, the fuel, and the timekeeper.

Why does this 'everything else' exist as its own subject? Because a fast engine surrounded by bad logistics is a slow car. Consider the sheer scale of the data involved. A scientific simulation of the weather, or a training run for a large language model (the kind of program that powers a chatbot), moves oceans of numbers between memory, chips, and separate computers. The pipes that carry those numbers are far narrower than the appetite of the chips at either end. When the pipe is the bottleneck, making the engine faster does nothing at all. So a huge amount of engineering goes into a single question: how do we send fewer numbers, send them more cleverly, or keep the chip busy while the numbers are in transit?

There is a second, subtler reason this chapter has to exist. A fast chip is not just fast; it is also expensive to build, expensive to power, and, it turns out, expensive to the planet. Making a chip requires enormous amounts of energy and rare materials in the factory, and running it burns electricity for years afterward. When you are trying to make computing 'better,' you have to first agree on what 'better' even means, and then measure it honestly. That sounds trivial. It is not. This chapter includes work showing that the field has been using a mathematically wrong formula to average its own speed measurements for decades, and work arguing that we should be optimizing for lifetime carbon footprint, not just raw speed. Before you can improve something, you must be able to measure it correctly, and that is genuinely hard.

A third strand is waste that hides in plain sight. The software that runs on these chips is built by stacking layers of other people's code, and each layer drags along mountains of features nobody in a given task will ever use. That unused code still has to be loaded into memory, shipped across the same narrow pipes, and stored on the same finite disks. It is dead weight riding along with the useful cargo. Trimming it is not exciting, but it directly relieves the same fundamental pressure: less to move, less to store, less to wait for.

Put it all together and a shape emerges. The headline chip is only as good as the logistics around it. This chapter is the study of those logistics: squeezing the data smaller so it fits through the pipe, spreading a job across many computers connected by slow links, cutting away the dead weight, measuring what we are doing without fooling ourselves, and counting the true cost. None of it is the engine. All of it decides whether the engine wins the race.

approaches.title: Squeeze the numbers smaller before you ship them
approaches.prose:
The most direct way to beat a narrow pipe is to send less through it. If a dataset is a billion numbers and you can rewrite it as half a billion numbers without losing any information, you have effectively doubled the width of every pipe and every disk it ever touches, for free. This is compression, and the trick is to find the hidden regularity in data and describe it more briefly. Most numbers in a scientific dataset are not random noise; neighboring measurements are similar, and the way computers store decimal numbers (a fixed format with a part for the scale and a part for the fine detail) leaves predictable patterns in the bits. A good compressor spots those patterns and encodes them compactly.

The hard part is that compression usually forces a painful trade. You can compress hard and slowly, getting a tiny file but making the chip wait while you pack and unpack it, which defeats the purpose. Or you can compress fast and loosely, keeping up with the chip but barely shrinking the file. Rarely do you get both. asplos-2025-017 tackles exactly this for scientific decimal data, designing compression methods that run on both kinds of chip (the flexible general-purpose chip and the massively parallel graphics-style chip) and that hit both goals at once: shrinking the data well while still packing and unpacking hundreds of gigabytes every second, fast enough to never stall the engine.

Crucially, this kind of compression is lossless, meaning you get back exactly what you put in, bit for bit. That matters for science, where throwing away detail can quietly corrupt a result. So the achievement is not just 'smaller,' but 'smaller, exact, and fast enough that it is always worth doing.' When that combination holds, compression becomes a free upgrade to every pipe in the system.

approaches.title: Spread the job across many computers, even when the wires between them are slow
approaches.prose:
Some jobs are simply too big for one machine. Training a large language model means adjusting billions of internal settings by showing the program mountains of text, over and over. No single chip has enough memory or enough time, so the work is split across hundreds or thousands of chips. But now the fundamental problem returns in a new form: those chips have to constantly compare notes with each other, and the wires connecting them are far slower than the chips themselves. If every chip has to stop and synchronize with every other chip at every tiny step, the whole cluster spends its life waiting on the network, and adding more chips stops helping.

There are two broad ways to fight this. The first is to synchronize less often. Instead of every chip reporting after each tiny step, let each one work independently for a long stretch, then combine everyone's progress occasionally. This slashes network traffic dramatically, at the risk that the chips drift apart and reach a worse answer. photon (mlsys-2025-036) shows this can actually work at the scale of billion-setting models, letting chips in different buildings or even different regions collaborate over ordinary internet-speed links by synchronizing hundreds of times less often, and remarkably ending up with a model as good as one trained the expensive centralized way. It even turns the noise from all that independent drifting into a mild benefit that helps the final model generalize.

The second way is to keep everyone busy while they wait, like an assembly line. Split the model into stages, hand each stage to a different chip, and keep a steady stream of work flowing so no stage sits idle waiting for the stage before it. The scheduling of this assembly line is surprisingly subtle: a naive schedule wastes memory and leaves chips idle, while a clever schedule overlaps computation and communication so the slow wires are hidden behind useful work. mlsys-2025-045 builds a system that lets researchers express these smarter assembly-line schedules easily, in a popular research framework that previously could only run the clumsy schedules. Both approaches share one goal: arrange the work so the slow links between machines stop being the thing everyone waits on.

approaches.title: Shrink the bookkeeping, not just the model
approaches.prose:
When you train one of these models, the actual settings you are trying to learn are only part of what has to live in the chip's precious, limited memory. The learning process itself keeps a running set of notes about how each setting has been changing, so it can adjust intelligently rather than blindly. The most popular learning method keeps two such notes for every single setting, which means the bookkeeping can take up two or three times as much memory as the model itself. For a model with billions of settings, that is tens of gigabytes of pure overhead, and it forces you onto more expensive chips or into slower, more awkward configurations.

The insight is that this bookkeeping is far more detailed than it needs to be. The learning method carefully tracks every setting individually, but you can get almost the same quality by tracking them in coarse groups, the way a manager can steer a large team by watching department-level trends instead of reading every employee's diary. apollo (mlsys-2025-059) approximates the per-setting notes with a much smaller summary, computed by squashing the information down into a compact form using a cheap mathematical shortcut rather than an expensive exact calculation. The result cuts the bookkeeping memory from tens of gigabytes down to a fraction of a gigabyte, with essentially no loss in the quality of the trained model.

Why does saving this memory matter so much? Because memory is the scarce resource that decides how much work a chip can do at once. Free up the memory the bookkeeping was hogging, and you can feed the chip much larger batches of data per step, which keeps it busy and can roughly triple how fast the whole training job runs. So this is not really about memory for its own sake; it is another route to the same destination, keeping the fast engine fed instead of starved.

approaches.title: Cut away the dead weight the software is dragging around
approaches.prose:
Modern software is built by stacking layers of code that other people wrote, each layer offering a huge menu of features so it can serve everybody. But any single task uses only a sliver of that menu. The rest is dead weight: code that never runs, yet still gets loaded into memory, shipped across the network when programs are deployed, and stored on disk. It is like moving house and shipping every appliance the manufacturer ever made, when you only use the toaster. This bloat quietly taxes the same scarce resources, memory, bandwidth, and storage, that everything else in this chapter is fighting to protect.

The fix is to watch what a program actually does and throw away everything it never touches. mlsys-2025-054 does exactly this for the big software packages behind machine learning. It observes which pieces of code are genuinely called when a real task runs, then surgically removes the vast unused remainder from the shipped software. The tricky part is doing this for the code that runs on the massively parallel graphics-style chips, which is bundled up opaquely and hard to inspect; the paper hooks into the moment each piece is requested to learn which pieces matter.

The payoffs are concrete and broad: the software files shrink by more than half, the memory footprint drops by roughly two-thirds, and programs even run meaningfully faster because there is less to load and manage. Nothing about the actual computation changed. The only thing that changed is how much useless cargo was riding along, which is a reminder that a surprising amount of computing cost is not the work itself but the weight of habits and defaults nobody questioned.

approaches.title: Do full-quality work only where it actually matters
approaches.prose:
A recurring way to save effort is to notice that not all of a task deserves the same care, and then spend your budget only where it counts. Human vision is a perfect example. Your eyes see fine detail only in a tiny central spot; everything to the sides is a blur you never consciously notice. So in a virtual-reality headset, rendering the entire scene in crisp full detail is mostly wasted, because the person can only actually resolve the small patch they are looking directly at. If you could track exactly where the eye is pointed, you could render that small patch sharply and the rest cheaply, and the person would never know the difference.

The catch is that this only pays off if the eye-tracking is itself cheap and fast. In a headset, everything must happen in a few thousandths of a second, or the person feels sick and the illusion breaks. A slow or power-hungry eye tracker would eat up all the savings it was supposed to create. isca-2025-108 solves this by designing the eye-tracking method and a small dedicated chip for it together, as one unit, so the tracking is fast and light enough that the rendering savings are real. Co-designing the algorithm and the hardware, rather than bolting a generic tracker onto a generic chip, is what makes the whole scheme add up to a large cut in the delay between looking and seeing.

The deeper principle generalizes far beyond headsets: find the part of the work that dominates the perceived result, pour your resources there, and skimp everywhere else. It is the computing equivalent of not repainting the walls behind the furniture. When the savings are large and the quality loss is invisible, this kind of selective effort is one of the highest-leverage moves available.

approaches.title: Reshape the work so the fast chip's strengths line up with the problem
approaches.prose:
The massively parallel graphics-style chip is astonishingly fast, but only when you feed it work shaped the way it likes: thousands of identical operations, all reading nearby data in lockstep. Give it a task shaped the wrong way and it stumbles, wasting most of its power. Many important jobs are naturally shaped wrong, so the art is to rearrange the same computation into a form the chip devours. Searching text for patterns, the thing behind 'find all phone numbers in this document,' is a classic example. Done the obvious way on a parallel chip, it reads the same chunk of text over and over for each pattern and each step, choking on the repeated fetching, which is our root problem yet again.

micro-2025-033 rearranges the search so each chunk of text is loaded exactly once and then run through every pattern and every step before moving on, dramatically cutting the fetching. This reordering is not free: steps that depend on earlier results now clash with the new order, so the work recomputes small dependency chains rather than pausing to pass messages between the chip's thousands of tiny workers, since recomputing is cheaper than coordinating. It also notices that huge stretches of the intermediate work turn out to be all-nothing and skips them entirely.

The common thread with the rest of this chapter is that the arithmetic did not change; the choreography did. By loading data once instead of many times, and by trading expensive coordination for cheap recomputation, the same search runs many times faster on the same chip. This is a recurring lesson: often the biggest speedups come not from a faster engine but from arranging the work so the engine never has to wait on the pipe.

approaches.title: Measure honestly, and count the true cost
approaches.prose:
Underneath all of this sits an unglamorous but essential discipline: if you cannot measure improvement correctly, you cannot reliably make it. It turns out this is where the field has been quietly fooling itself. When researchers test a new chip on many different programs, they get many separate speed numbers and must boil them down to one summary figure. The standard way of averaging those figures, used for decades, is mathematically wrong for this kind of ratio, and can even declare the slower of two designs to be the faster one. hpca-2025-025 works out from first principles the correct way to average speedups and shows concrete cases where the old habit points to the wrong conclusion. It is a sobering reminder that a whole field can march confidently in a slightly wrong direction if its ruler is bent.

The other honesty problem is about cost, specifically the cost to the planet. A chip is expensive to the environment twice over: once in the factory, which burns enormous energy and consumes rare materials to build it, and again over its whole working life as it draws electricity. Chasing raw speed alone can lead you to build a monster that is fast but ruinously costly to make and run. hpca-2025-026 proposes a single honest yardstick that folds together the carbon from building the chip, the carbon from running it, and how fast it actually gets work done, so designers can trade these off deliberately instead of ignoring the ones that do not show up on a benchmark.

These measurement papers are the timekeeper and the accountant of the whole enterprise. They produce no faster chip themselves, but they decide whether everyone else's claims of 'faster' and 'better' are even true. In a field driven by numbers, getting the numbers right, and counting the costs that are easy to leave out, is quietly one of the most consequential things you can do.

where_it_stands:
The pieces here are individually strong but deliberately scattered, because they are the 'everything else' that surrounds the headline chips rather than a single unified push. On the solved side, the mechanics are impressive and real: you can compress scientific data losslessly at hundreds of gigabytes per second, train billion-setting models across slow internet links and still match centralized quality, cut a learning method's memory overhead by more than an order of magnitude, and strip more than half the dead weight out of machine-learning software. Each of these directly relieves the root pressure of moving and storing data, and each is close to something a practitioner could adopt today.

What remains open is harder and more foundational. We still lack agreed, honest ways to measure what we are doing: a whole subfield has been averaging its speed numbers with the wrong formula, and counting the true lifetime carbon cost of hardware is only just being taken seriously, with the metrics and data still immature. Many of the biggest wins here come from co-designing an algorithm and a chip together for one narrow task, which works beautifully but does not generalize, so every new problem needs its own bespoke effort. And the deepest gap is that all of this is treatment, not cure: these are clever ways to send fewer numbers and hide the waiting, but the fundamental gulf between how fast chips compute and how slowly data moves between them keeps widening, which means the pit crew has to keep getting better just to keep the race competitive.
